---
title: "Small grammar checks"
subtitle: "Score three checks and keep the limits visible"
description: "Learn how small grammar checks can find planted errors and why they are not a full grammar checker."
categories: [sentences and paragraphs, grammar checking, workforce research]
---

The coordinator cannot approve a public summary from spelling alone. Correctly
spelled words can still form ungrammatical sentences.

A spelling check compares words with accepted spellings. **Grammar** concerns
how words combine in sentences. This lesson builds three small checks for
sentences with deliberately inserted errors.

This project does not install a grammar checker, so the lesson builds three
small checks by hand and treats them as a demonstration. Offline means the check
uses local files, without sending text to a web service.

::: {.callout-note}
The Riverton sentences and marked grammar examples are invented for this lesson.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- explain the difference between spelling and grammar checks.
- use UDPipe dependency output to compare a subject and a verb.
- find doubled words with a stringr pattern.
- compare a simple `a` and `an` rule with expected answers.
- explain why a demonstration check is not a working grammar checker.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false

options(warn = 2)
stopifnot(identical(getOption("warn"), 2L))
```

## Make a marked test set

readr reads the Riverton CSV. tokenizers and purrr prepare words, stringr does
two pattern checks, and a local udpipe parser processes sentences. dplyr and
tibble organize the results. A **dependency parser** gives labels to grammatical
relationships, such as the relation between a verb and its subject.

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(purrr)
library(stringr)
library(tokenizers)
library(udpipe)

sentences <- read_csv(
  "data/workforce/workforce_sentences.csv",
  na = character(),
  col_types = cols(
    sentence_id = col_character(),
    document_id = col_character(),
    source_line = col_character(),
    text = col_character(),
    reference_label = col_character(),
    uncertainty = col_character(),
    annotator_id = col_character(),
    rationale = col_character(),
    codebook_version = col_character(),
    codebook_hash = col_character(),
    derived = col_character(),
    transformation = col_character()
  )
)

marked_sentences <- tibble(
  example_id = sprintf("g%02d", 1:14),
  text = c(
    "The worker checks the list.",
    "The worker check the list.",
    "The applicants submit forms.",
    "The applicants submits forms.",
    "Bring a badge to orientation.",
    "Bring a envelope to orientation.",
    "Apply for an evening class.",
    "Apply for a evening class.",
    "The session begins in an hour.",
    "A university partner sends trainers.",
    "The coordinator checks the the form.",
    "The team needs needs support.",
    "The employee uses a spreadsheet.",
    "The employee use a spreadsheet."
  ),
  planted_check = c(
    "none",
    "subject-verb number",
    "none",
    "subject-verb number",
    "none",
    "article letters",
    "none",
    "article letters",
    "none",
    "none",
    "doubled word",
    "doubled word",
    "none",
    "subject-verb number"
  )
) |>
  mutate(has_planted_error = planted_check != "none")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  marked_sentences,
  col.names = c("Example ID", "Sentence", "Planted check", "Has planted error"),
  caption = "Author-marked sentences before the checks",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(all(c(
  "readr", "dplyr", "tibble", "purrr", "stringr", "tokenizers", "udpipe"
) %in% loadedNamespaces()))

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(sentences), 28L),
  identical(nrow(marked_sentences), 14L),
  identical(sum(marked_sentences$has_planted_error), 7L),
  identical(sum(!marked_sentences$has_planted_error), 7L),
  identical(sum(marked_sentences$planted_check == "subject-verb number"), 3L),
  identical(sum(marked_sentences$planted_check == "doubled word"), 2L),
  identical(sum(marked_sentences$planted_check == "article letters"), 2L)
)
```

The author marks seven of the 14 test sentences as correct. The other seven
each contain one planted error. Success on these examples does not establish
general grammar-checking performance.

## Do the three checks

The subject-verb check uses the UDPipe parser's `feats` column, which can contain
values such as `Number=Sing` or `Number=Plur`. It searches for an `nsubj` relation,
short for nominal subject, pointing to a verb. In the code, `\(tokens)` is R
shorthand for a small function applied to one sentence's tokens.

```{r}
extract_number <- function(feats) {
  str_match(coalesce(feats, ""), "Number=([^|]+)")[, 2]
}

find_subject_verb_flags <- function(annotated) {
  annotated_with_number <- annotated |>
    mutate(number = extract_number(feats))

  subjects <- annotated_with_number |>
    filter(dep_rel == "nsubj") |>
    transmute(
      doc_id,
      head_token_id,
      subject_token = token,
      subject_number = number
    )

  verbs <- annotated_with_number |>
    filter(upos %in% c("VERB", "AUX"), !is.na(number)) |>
    transmute(
      doc_id,
      verb_token_id = token_id,
      verb_token = token,
      verb_number = number
    )

  verbs |>
    inner_join(subjects, by = c("doc_id", "verb_token_id" = "head_token_id")) |>
    mutate(flag = !is.na(subject_number) & subject_number != verb_number)
}

score_check <- function(flag, expected) {
  tibble(
    true_positive = sum(flag & expected),
    false_positive = sum(flag & !expected),
    false_negative = sum(!flag & expected),
    true_negative = sum(!flag & !expected)
  )
}

parser <- udpipe_load_model("data/treebank/en_ewt-500-parser.udpipe")

marked_vertical <- marked_sentences$text |>
  tokenize_words(lowercase = FALSE, strip_punct = FALSE) |>
  map_chr(\(tokens) paste(tokens, collapse = "\n"))

marked_annotated <- udpipe_annotate(
  parser,
  x = marked_vertical,
  doc_id = marked_sentences$example_id,
  tokenizer = "vertical",
  tagger = "default",
  parser = "default"
) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  as_tibble()

agreement_pairs <- find_subject_verb_flags(marked_annotated)
agreement_flags <- agreement_pairs |>
  summarise(agreement_flag = any(flag), .by = doc_id)

doubled_pattern <- regex("\\b([[:alpha:]]+)\\s+\\1\\b", ignore_case = TRUE)
article_pattern <- regex(
  "\\b(a)\\s+[aeiou][[:alpha:]]*|\\b(an)\\s+[^aeiou\\W][[:alpha:]]*",
  ignore_case = TRUE
)

scored_examples <- marked_sentences |>
  left_join(agreement_flags, by = c("example_id" = "doc_id")) |>
  mutate(
    agreement_flag = coalesce(agreement_flag, FALSE),
    doubled_flag = str_detect(text, doubled_pattern),
    article_flag = str_detect(text, article_pattern)
  )

check_scores <- bind_rows(
  score_check(
    scored_examples$agreement_flag,
    scored_examples$planted_check == "subject-verb number"
  ) |>
    mutate(check = "subject-verb number"),
  score_check(
    scored_examples$doubled_flag,
    scored_examples$planted_check == "doubled word"
  ) |>
    mutate(check = "doubled word"),
  score_check(
    scored_examples$article_flag,
    scored_examples$planted_check == "article letters"
  ) |>
    mutate(check = "article letters")
) |>
  select(check, everything())

expected_scores <- tibble(
  check = c("subject-verb number", "doubled word", "article letters"),
  true_positive = c(3L, 2L, 2L),
  false_positive = c(0L, 0L, 2L),
  false_negative = c(0L, 0L, 0L),
  true_negative = c(11L, 12L, 10L)
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  agreement_pairs |>
    select(doc_id, subject_token, subject_number, verb_token, verb_number, flag),
  col.names = c("Example ID", "Subject", "Subject number", "Verb", "Verb number", "Flagged"),
  caption = "Subject-verb pairs found by the dependency parser",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  check_scores,
  col.names = c("Check", "True positives", "False positives", "False negatives", "True negatives"),
  caption = "Scores for the three grammar checks on marked examples",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(
    scored_examples$example_id[scored_examples$agreement_flag],
    c("g02", "g04", "g14")
  ),
  identical(
    scored_examples$example_id[scored_examples$doubled_flag],
    c("g11", "g12")
  ),
  identical(
    scored_examples$example_id[scored_examples$article_flag],
    c("g06", "g08", "g09", "g10")
  ),
  identical(check_scores, expected_scores)
)
```

The checks and expected answers share an author, so the score is a teaching
check rather than an accuracy estimate. A true positive is a planted error that a
check puts a mark on. A false positive is a correct sentence that a check puts a
mark on. A false negative is a planted error that a check misses. A true
negative is a correct sentence it leaves alone.

The subject-verb number check finds all three planted number errors in this
small set. The doubled-word check finds both repeated-word examples. The
article check finds the two planted `a` mistakes but also puts a mark on the
correct phrases `an hour` and `A university`.

That rule uses the first letter, while English article choice depends on
sound. `Hour` begins with a vowel sound because its h is silent.
`University` begins with a consonant y sound. The rule uses letters without
pronunciation information.

A real grammar checker uses thousands of rules, a trained model, or both. These
three checks demonstrate the idea. The project trains its deliberately weak
UDPipe model on 500 sentences. Model errors can affect every subject-verb
result. The article rule deliberately contains an error to demonstrate its
failure.

## Try the Riverton sentences

The code applies the same three checks to the 28 Riverton sentences. The
output selects sentences for a person to examine. It does not prove that
sentences without a mark are correct.

```{r}
riverton_vertical <- sentences$text |>
  tokenize_words(lowercase = FALSE, strip_punct = FALSE) |>
  map_chr(\(tokens) paste(tokens, collapse = "\n"))

riverton_annotated <- udpipe_annotate(
  parser,
  x = riverton_vertical,
  doc_id = sentences$sentence_id,
  tokenizer = "vertical",
  tagger = "default",
  parser = "default"
) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  as_tibble()

riverton_agreement_pairs <- find_subject_verb_flags(riverton_annotated)
riverton_agreement_ids <- riverton_agreement_pairs |>
  filter(flag) |>
  pull(doc_id)
riverton_pair_sentence_count <- n_distinct(riverton_agreement_pairs$doc_id)

riverton_flags <- sentences |>
  transmute(
    sentence_id,
    text,
    agreement_flag = sentence_id %in% riverton_agreement_ids,
    doubled_flag = str_detect(text, doubled_pattern),
    article_flag = str_detect(text, article_pattern)
  ) |>
  mutate(any_flag = agreement_flag | doubled_flag | article_flag)

riverton_flag_summary <- tibble(
  check = c("subject-verb number", "doubled word", "article letters", "any check"),
  flagged_sentences = c(
    sum(riverton_flags$agreement_flag),
    sum(riverton_flags$doubled_flag),
    sum(riverton_flags$article_flag),
    sum(riverton_flags$any_flag)
  )
)

riverton_coverage <- tibble(
  measure = c("sentences with subject-verb pair", "sentences without subject-verb pair"),
  sentences = c(
    riverton_pair_sentence_count,
    nrow(sentences) - riverton_pair_sentence_count
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  riverton_flag_summary,
  col.names = c("Check", "Flagged Riverton sentences"),
  caption = "Grammar-check flags in the 28 Riverton sentences",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  riverton_coverage,
  col.names = c("Coverage measure", "Sentences"),
  caption = "Subject-verb coverage in the Riverton sentences",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(riverton_agreement_pairs), 4L),
  identical(riverton_coverage$sentences, c(4L, 24L)),
  identical(riverton_flag_summary$flagged_sentences, c(0L, 0L, 0L, 0L)),
  identical(sum(riverton_flags$any_flag), 0L),
  identical(nrow(riverton_flags), 28L)
)
```

No check puts a mark on a Riverton sentence. The subject-verb check finds only
four subject-and-verb pairs in all 28 sentences. It requires a number feature
on the verb, which English verbs rarely have. It cannot evaluate the other
24 sentences. Zero flags therefore mainly reflect limited coverage, not
correctness.

## Grammar checking in production

The three custom checks demonstrate the concept rather than provide a complete
offline grammar checker. Established open-source tools such as LanguageTool
provide broader functionality. Production systems distinguish these issues:

- **Detection vs. correction**: Marking a possible error is safer than automatically rewriting text, particularly when the detector covers few error types.
- **Normative context and auditability**: Grammar conventions depend on the intended style, such as formal business English or informal messages. Rule-based systems can explain each flag through a named rule. Deep learning models can suggest fluent corrections but often cannot explain the convention behind each suggestion.
- **Rule/model/error-type comparison**: Rule-based engines can precisely detect local style and typing errors, such as doubled words or wrong articles. Neural models generally address semantic confusion in sentences whose grammatical structure appears valid.

## What to remember

- Spelling checks examine words. Grammar checks examine word relationships.
- A small subject-verb check can use UDPipe's `feats` and `nsubj` labels.
- A doubled-word pattern is simple and useful for one common typo.
- The article-letter rule falsely puts a mark on `an hour` and `A university`.
- These three checks are demonstrations, not an offline grammar checker for R.
- No Riverton flags here means low coverage, not clean grammar.

The three checks can select sentences for a person to examine. They cannot
approve public text independently. The subject-verb check covers only four
Riverton sentences.
